title: EU carbon price without border adjustment leaked emissions to coal neighbours
programme: EU Emissions Trading System (no border carbon adjustment on electricity imports)
problem: EU generators pay the ETS carbon price, but electricity imported from neighbours with zero or near-zero carbon pricing does not, giving coal plants across the border a cost advantage.
solution: The EU ETS priced power-sector emissions only inside the bloc. Sandbag proposes a border carbon adjustment on gross electricity imports until each trading partner adopts an equivalent carbon price.
results: Net electricity imports into the EU ETS region rose from 3TWh in 2017 to 21TWh in 2019. The imports emitted an estimated 26 million tonnes of CO2 and avoided €630m of carbon costs in 2019.
serbia_reason: Serbian lignite power is the kind of unpriced coal electricity this report found flowing into the EU, and the border adjustment it proposed is what CBAM now does. Serbia's electricity exports are directly exposed.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need its own carbon price and verified emissions data so that the EU border charge on its electricity is reduced or waived.
blockers: A domestic carbon price raises costs for lignite generation and puts pressure on household tariffs that are politically sensitive.
quote: Coal power plants just outside European borders are supplying electricity to the EU while avoiding the carbon price. We reveal that countries covered by the EU carbon price are increasingly importing electricity, and many new links are planned.

title: Spain's coal decline partly offset by rising Moroccan coal power imports
problem: As Spain cut its domestic coal generation, the interconnector to Morocco let unpriced coal power from across the border fill part of the gap.
solution: Spain reduced coal-fired generation and set a draft NECP target of 74% renewable electricity by 2030, while more interconnection with Morocco is planned.
results: Between 2018 and 2019 Spain cut domestic coal generation by 25TWh but net imports from Morocco rose by 4TWh. On average the imported power was twice as carbon intensive as Spain's own supply.
serbia_reason: Closing coal at home while importing coal power from a neighbour with no carbon price only moves emissions elsewhere. Serbia is on the exporting side of this pattern with its EU neighbours.
adapt_needed: Serbia would have to plan coal closures together with its interconnection and import strategy, so that domestic lignite is not simply replaced by imported coal power.
blockers: Serbia's neighbours also run coal plants without carbon prices, so cheap coal imports would remain available.
quote: Between 2018 and 2019, Spain reduced domestic coal generation by 25TWh, yet increased net imports from Morocco by 4TWh. This is a clear sign of carbon leakage.

title: Serbia's planned new coal units deepen its carbon-leakage exposure
programme: Serbia INDC and planned coal power units
problem: Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, among the most carbon-intensive grids connected to the EU, were planning new coal capacity while their EU neighbours decarbonise.
solution: Serbia planned about 2GW of new coal capacity and pledged only a 10% GHG emissions cut by 2030 in its INDC.
results: Coal projects totalling 6.3GW were at some stage of planning in the Western Balkans, an 86% increase on the 7.3GW operating, with most of the non-Bosnian share in Serbia. Western Balkan power sent to the EU in 2019 emitted an estimated 5.2MtCO2, 20% of the CO2 from all EU electricity imports.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own plan to build more lignite capacity for a grid that is strongly connected to the EU. The report argues such imports should face a border carbon price, which is how CBAM now works.
adapt_needed: New generation planning in Serbia would need to price in an EU border carbon charge on exports and test low-carbon alternatives before new lignite units.
blockers: Lignite is cheap domestic fuel and underpins energy security arguments for new units.
quote: The remaining planned coal capacity is mostly in Serbia, which has a similar share of renewable electricity to Bosnia & Herzegovina, and has pledged to reduce GHG emissions by 10% by 2030.

title: Ukraine's very low carbon tax and stalled ETS barely priced coal exports
programme: Ukraine carbon tax and EU Association Agreement ETS obligation
problem: Ukrainian exports to Hungary, Poland and Slovakia come almost entirely from coal plants, but face a carbon price that is a tiny fraction of the EU's.
solution: Under its EU Association Agreement Ukraine committed to develop an emissions trading scheme within two years of entry into force, and it runs a carbon tax that applies to power generation.
results: The Association Agreement entered into force on 1 September 2017 but the ETS had not materialised by the time of writing. From 1 January 2019 the carbon tax rose to only UAH10/tCO2 (€0.31/tCO2), while EU ETS allowances cost about €25/tCO2 in 2019.
serbia_reason: Serbia also has EU-linked obligations to align carbon pricing and plans to start with a low carbon tax. Ukraine shows that a token price and a missed ETS deadline leave coal exports exposed to the EU border.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a credible timetable that raises its carbon price towards EU levels, rather than a symbolic rate.
blockers: Raising the carbon price quickly would hit lignite generators and consumer tariffs.
quote: This scheme is yet to materialise. Ukraine does however have a functioning carbon tax, which applies to power generation.
